3181.tone: Faraclas & Ramirez Morales 2006 (excerpt) re-analyse word prominence in Crucian and other Afro-Caribbean English-lexifier creoles as an H(L) tone melody assigned, after Devonish 2002, to the syllable that carries stress in the English citation form; they call ACELC dialects 'to some extent tonal', show Crucian downdrift and utterance-final tonal effects (wúmàn, próféshnàl), and report both downdrift and final cadence. 3182.prule: Stem (root)-syllable stress in simple and derived native words, unmoved by inflection or derivation: Vercouillie states 'the laws of stress are the same as in Dutch' and follows Brill §§ 41-45, whose § 42 puts the stress 'op de stamsyllabe' (édel, vertéllen, gehóórzaamheid); compounds stressed on the determining (first) member (hóogepriester, stádhuis, búrgemeester; place names A'msterdam, Bréda, Déndermonde). West Flemish differs from Dutch chiefly by applying the general stem/initial rule where Dutch has exceptions, notably loans with initial stress (áltaar, pástoor, sálpeter, tábak, bárometer, thérmometer). Position is set by morphological structure (stem vs. affix, determining member of compound), not by syllable count or weight.
3182.srule: By reference only: Vercouillie 1885 says the stress laws are those of Dutch and follows Brill 1849 §§ 41-45, adding no West Flemish particulars under Brill's § 44 'bijtoon'; Brill § 44 puts the secondary stress (bijtoon) on the stem syllable of words with a main-stressed prefix or suffix (áárts-schèlm, kòningín, vìjándelijk), on full-vowel suffixes (dánkbaàr, jóngelìng, óefenìng) and, in compounds, on the stem syllable of the member without main stress (níeuwjaàr, dáglìcht); schwa syllables and inflections toneless. Vercouillie's only doubly marked form, dértiendàagsch (acute + grave), fits § 44.3; he does not use the word bijtoon and his grave is not systematic (dertièndag).

3183.prule: 'Categorial' (morphologically determined) accent: no fixed syllable position (stress attested on 1st-4th syllables of the word form) and no weight criterion; the position of stress in every word form follows from the word's inflectional type and lexical stratum. Each morpheme has an accentual strength (unstressed A / potentially stressed À / obligatorily stressed Ȁ) and, for polysyllabic morphemes, a fixed stressed syllable; the 'contour rule' puts word stress on the strongest morpheme, rightmost among equals (stress 'strives rightward'). Concretely: stratum-I (inherited) nouns/adjectives/pronouns stress the direct-case ending or, with zero ending, the last stem syllable (tirvò, řòm); stratum-II (loan) nominals stress a lexically fixed stem syllable in direct forms (kòkalo, paramìći, harambàš); oblique endings are always stressed (tirvès, kokalòn); vocative pl. on the first syllable of the ending; verbs fall in three mobility classes (always final; stem-stressed in the present but final in the perfect; always on the same suffix); postfixes, articles, most prepositions, conjunctions and enclitics are never stressed.
3183.srule: None within the narrow word form: 'узкой словоформы, могущей иметь максимум одно ударение' (a narrow word form can have at most one stress). 3185.prule: Word-accent (accented syllables bear high pitch, unaccented low) is predictable and anchored to the stem-initial syllable of the phonological word: 'A phonological word is defined as one whose stem-initial syllable is prominent.' In unprefixed words (nominals, adverbs, most of the lexicon) the stem-initial syllable is the word-initial syllable, so accent is initial there. In prefixed verbs 'pitch-raising spreads leftwards from the initial syllable of the stem' over the pronominal and derivational prefixes, so the accented (high) span runs from the word-initial syllable to the stem-initial syllable and its extent is set by the stem boundary, not by syllable count; inflectional and derivational suffixes and enclitics are unaccented (low). No weight condition; no lexical contrast stated.
3185.srule: Not mentioned in Ford 1990, sec. 2.5 'Word-accent and sentence intonation', pp. 40-43 (read in full): only an accented (high) / unaccented (low) distinction; the several high syllables on prefixed verbs are leftward pitch-spread from the stem-initial syllable within the one word-accent, not a secondary accent.

3186.heavy: (a) 'संयुक्त व्यंजन के पूर्व का स्वर' -- the vowel before a conjunct consonant, including nasal+consonant (अद्दर, लुस्सौ, रंग, भंग, संपल); (b) a syllable with आ/ए/ओ as against one with अ/इ/उ (करे, दलासौ, बलाडु: stress on the आ/ए/ओ syllable after a short first syllable); a final 'silent' अ or open इ/उ is light. Cy clusters (कर्यु) do not make the preceding अ/इ/उ syllable heavy. The source states the vowel contrast by vowel identity, not by the word 'length'.
3186.dflt: initial (penult in disyllables: rule ३ अ; initial in trisyllables: rule ४, 'सामान्यतया')
3186.prule: Weak, non-contrastive dynamic word stress, weight-conditioned: (1) monosyllables always stressed; (2) in polysyllables the vowel before a conjunct consonant, incl. nasal+C, is always stressed (closed syllable = heavy); (3a) disyllables whose final syllable has silent अ or open इ/उ stress the penult; (3b) disyllables with अ/इ/उ in the first syllable and ए/ओ in the final stress the final; (4) trisyllables take primary stress on the initial and secondary on the final, but if the first syllable has अ/इ/उ and the second आ/ए/ओ the second is stressed. Net: stress the leftmost heavy syllable (closed, or with आ/ए/ओ) among the first two, default initial.
3186.srule: Joshi distinguishes secondary (द्वैतीयिक) from primary stress: in trisyllables with initial primary stress the secondary falls on the final syllable (kutru, dikro, satri); secondary stress is 'also expressed at the appropriate place in words of more syllables' (placement beyond three syllables not given); it moves when a syllable is added (āḷas: secondary on -ḷas; āḷsu: on -su, primary staying on ā-); in y-cluster words whose first syllable has ā/e/o the y-syllable carries only secondary stress (kāḍyu, mānyu, bolyu).

3188.prule: Default accent (non-contrastive raised pitch) on the final syllable of the word; forms with certain suffixes keep the accent on the final syllable of the stem instead of the suffix, the excluded class being inflectional or enclitic suffixes (Strand 2007/2016: 'accent falls automatically on a word's final syllable (excluding inflectional or enclitic suffixes)'). Position therefore follows from word and morphological boundaries (suffix class) rather than from the word's syllable count alone; weight plays no role.

3189.dq: bijna alle woorden den klemtoon krijgen op de 3e lettergreep van achteren
3189.dloc: p. 33 (p. 44 of archive.org item tijdschriftvoor13zendgoog), the remark heading the Tab./Wai./Ib./Gal./Lod. comparative word lists; accent-marked Waioli forms in the lists pp. 33-36
3189.prule: Default stress on the antepenultimate syllable (the 3rd syllable from the end), counted from the right edge and blind to syllable weight; stated as one blanket rule over all the compared varieties except Galela and Ternate, i.e. covering the Waioli column together with Tabaru, Ibu and Loda. Words that deviate carry an acute in the lists. The marked Waioli deviations on pp. 34-36 are 11 distinct types (12 list entries, weré'a appearing under two glosses; the tens on p. 34 repeat romodídi/roánge/romotóo under ditto marks): romodídi '2', roánge '3', romotóo '5', tumudíngi '7', ja midídi / ja duánge '2/3 persons', kaúna 'dog', tubaíe 'youth', weré'a 'wife/woman', ngáu'u 'ear', kailáu 'sarong'. Most are penultimate; ngáu'u and kailáu are penultimate only if 'au' is read as two syllables, and Fortgens' marking of the parallel Tab. ngáuku (redundant under a three-syllable reading) suggests he counts 'au' as one syllable, on which reading kailáu is final-stressed. Disyllables are not covered by the rule (antepenult impossible) and are left unmarked (banjo 'water', oti 'canoe', rata '4', rimoi '1').

3191.prule: Dynamic (силовое) stress on the LAST syllable of nominals (nouns, adjectives, other non-verbal words) and deverbal nouns; every derivational suffix carries the stress to the new final syllable (kitkán > kitkanə́k > kitkandunə́k). Weight plays no role. Inflectional endings, suffixal function elements, enclitics and the noun plural markers -išt/-əv never take stress, so the domain is the derivational stem (δə́γ̌d-išt, wúz-əm x̌átəy). Steblin-Kamensky 1999 §75 concurs: all words other than verb forms and some grammatical markers have fixed stress, on the last syllable of disyllables (native words are mono- or disyllabic).

3192.prule: Morpheme-inherent (lexical) stress: every Sahaptin lexical morpheme carries its own inherent stress whose position is not derivable from any rule (no positional default; explicitly contrasted with the Nez Perce penultimate rule for words without inherent stress). Three levels of stress; only primary is written.

3197.tone: Source: three levels of tone realization corresponding to four underlying tones; minimal pairs gú 'genet species' / gū 'shrub species' / gù 'hunger'; the 'neutral-high' tone is realized H, M or L depending on syntactic position and neighbouring tones (within 'tonally compact' constituents it copies the preceding tone before a following H/neutral-high, else surfaces H; outside them it surfaces M before H/neutral-high within the same maximal phrase group, else H); two adjacent H tones usually realized with a raise on the second; second and later H/neutral-high tones lowered to L inside tonally compact constituents; contour tones unattested; final L may fall; H is lower after a preceding L (downdrift-like); past tense of most monosyllabic verbs marked by replacement of lexical tone with M. Ravenhill 1982 (Kemu dialect) likewise gives three level tones and never mentions stress or accent (only 'acute/grave accent' as tone diacritics).

3198.dq: The phonemic status of stress, here and elsewhere, has not been completely investigated. However, there is no evidence that it is phonemic, and in at least some phrases there appears to be some freedom in the position of stress.
3198.dloc: Section 1.9.4 (Phonology: morphologically complex rising and falling tones), p. 24 of the original pagination
3198.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Three-toneme (level H/M/L, plus falling and rare rising tones) tone language; the only remark on stress is phonetic and local: in Wukari (Wapan) the beginning of a morphologically derived rising-tone glide is stressed (Takum: the end). Stress is said to have no evidence of phonemic status and to show some freedom of position in at least some phrases.
3198.quote: In every instance of these tone glides, the end of the glide is morphologically an alternant of a prefix /á/ (in both dialects) or /a/ (Wukari only). The vowel of this prefix drops when another word precedes. ... An interesting dialect difference is that in Takum it is the end of a rising tone that is stressed, while in Wukari it is the beginning that is stressed. Thus forms from the two dialects which are identical in tone are quite different in stress. The phonemic status of stress, here and elsewhere, has not been completely investigated. However, there is no evidence that it is phonemic, …
3198.loc: Section 1.9.4 (Phonology: morphologically complex rising and falling tones), p. 24 of the original pagination

The book describes both in parallel; in the quoted passage only…
3198.exq_: The phonemic status of stress, here and elsewhere, has not been completely investigated.
3198.tone: Welmers 1.9: 'The two dialects have the same tonemes, although the distribution of these tonemes in relation to morphemes is quite different in the two.' 1.9.1 gives the three level tonemes (scan of the heading is partial: 'The three...'; the compilers read H/M/L from the page), 1.9.2 falling tones (Takum noun stems; Wukari pronouns in final position), 1.9.3 a rare rising tone, 1.9.4 the morphophonemic rising/falling glides at word junctures where the dropped prefix vowel surfaces as the glide end. 1.10: 'Both dialects have two intonemes which affect the end of an utterance'; the interrogative intoneme 'includes a lengthening of the final syllable', with Wukari final high dropping to about mid. Stress is mentioned only in the 1.9.4 passage quoted: non-phonemic, locally anchored to the start of a rising glide in Wukari, positionally somewhat free in phrases.

3205.prule: Authors' statement: stress is not phonemic and its placement cannot be predicted; in disyllables it falls sometimes on the 1st, sometimes on the 2nd syllable; in trisyllables 'generally' on the 2nd; in 4- and 5-syllable words 'generally' on the 3rd and 4th respectively (a penult-like tendency, hedged with 'pada umumnya', never stated as a rule). Net: non-contrastive stress with competing patterns (penult-type prose vs a peninitial 01 010 0100 pattern in the transcriptions that the authors never state) and no rule the source itself commits to.

3206.heavy: p.136: "the 'heavier' cluster attracts stress, but the 'lighter' one does not": a tri-consonantal cluster (p.117: liquid or /j/ + nasal + non-apico-alveolar stop) attracts stress to its first phoneme, i.e. the syllable closed by the cluster's sonorant first member (e.g. /jajnja-n/ [dzaíndzan], /gulgura-j-n-gan/ [gołgoraíngan], scan '/guigura-j-n-gan/'); a bi-consonantal cluster does not (stress stays initial, p.135); p.140: the long vowel [i:] (phonetic brackets in the source; p.1 lists 'three short vowels, and one long vowel') 'outranks a tri-consonantal cluster'. A plain closed syllable is NOT heavy: [gá.mon.ga], [bí.mo.gan], [bál.gan] keep initial stress. Heavy class as stated: CVV, and CVC/CVCC only when its coda opens a CCC cluster. No standard weight enum matches
3206.dflt: word-initial syllable (p.134 'In the main, stress tends to fall on the word-initial syllable. This is the most dominant tendency.'; p.135 with a bi-consonantal cluster 'stress falls on the first syllable of the word')
3206.prule: Non-distinctive phonetic stress (p.133). Default: the word-initial syllable ('In the main, stress tends to fall on the word-initial syllable. This is the most dominant tendency', p.134). A 'heavier' syllable draws stress off the default: when a word contains a tri-consonantal cluster (liquid or /j/ + nasal + stop, p.117), 'stress shifts to the first phoneme of the tri-consonantal cluster' (pp.136-137), i.e. onto the syllable closed by the cluster's sonorant first member (the /j/ surfacing as vocalic [i], e.g. [dzaíndzan], [gołgoraíngan]); with a bi-consonantal cluster stress stays on the first syllable (p.135); the long vowel [i:] 'outranks a tri-consonantal cluster' (p.140). Certain suffixes (not all) additionally shift stress to the following vowel (pp.136-139). Exceptions with 'reason... not known' (p.136, e.g. /bujnjul/ [boindʒól], scan [boingjól]) and non-initial residue (p.141). No per-length fixed grid is stated.
3206.srule: Only in complex forms: in compounds, secondary stress on the first syllable of the first root (primary on the first syllable of the second root; 'There appears to be no exception', e.g. /julaj-nungul/ [dzòlainóngol], p.135); in the reduplicated verb /bajabajanan/ [bátfabátfanan] the stress on the second copy 'may be secondary stress' (p.135); in two-word placenames, secondary stress on the first syllable of the first word (p.24). Simple polysyllables are transcribed with one stress ([dólobo], [jambábara], [balgágalen], [gołgoraíngan]); no rhythmic secondary stress is described in the text seen (full pp.133-141 not seen; excerpt grade).
